body_paragraphs: Yesterday's Trump-Netanyahu meeting lasted about as long as the calm it produced. Overnight, Iran's Revolutionary Guard says it struck US bases in Jordan and elsewhere across the Gulf; Trump has vowed to hit back hard and repeated a threat to bomb Iran's bridges. Brent crude, which had eased into the mid-to-high $80s by Tuesday, jumped back above $90 in early trading - close to the fourth or fifth version of this same story in three weeks.

That reversal lands hours before the Fed's own decision, due at 2 PM. Hike odds had already climbed toward 38% by this morning, one of the sharpest run-ups on record for a single meeting, and this morning's oil spike gives the committee one more inflation input it can't fully control, right before it has to vote. Whatever they decide, they're deciding into real uncertainty, not a settled picture.

Closer to home: Miami has actually won two straight, not the one game reported here yesterday - Monday's walk-off was real, but Tuesday's was a separate 1-0 shutout behind Alcantara, and the record got tangled in the retelling. They host the series finale at 12:10. And if you want a quieter counterweight tonight: a sculptor in New Mexico just finished a naked-eye observatory he started fifty years ago.

rabbit_hole.title: Artist Charles Ross Spent 50 Years Trying to Bring the Stars Down to Earth. At 88, Has He Done It?
rabbit_hole.creator: Artnet News
rabbit_hole.why: Today's exploration pick, deliberately outside markets, Miami, and sports: Charles Ross broke ground on 'Star Axis' - a naked-eye observatory built into a New Mexico mesa, aligned to the 26,000-year cycle of Earth's axis - in 1971, and it's only now, at 88, nearing completion. Worth the sit as a counterweight to a day built entirely out of overnight reversals: a single vision, held for fifty years, that never once needed the news to cooperate.

beautiful_thing.title: The Freedom Tower
beautiful_thing.creator: Schultze & Weaver, architects
beautiful_thing.body: Schultze & Weaver - the firm behind New York's Waldorf-Astoria and the Biltmore in Coral Gables - designed this Mediterranean Revival tower in downtown Miami as the home of the Miami News, modeling its campanile on the Giralda bell tower in Seville. It sat largely unused after the paper moved out in 1957 until the federal government leased it from 1962 to 1974 to process and assist more than 400,000 Cuban refugees fleeing Castro's government, earning it the name 'the Ellis Island of the South.' It was designated a National Historic Landmark in 2008 and now belongs to Miami Dade College, which uses it as a museum and cultural center.
